grammar_points.name: 〜ば (conditional)

explanation.en:
How it works: Change the verb ending to form an 'if' condition. For -ru verbs (ichidan), replace る with れば. For -u verbs (godan), change the final syllable to its え-row equivalent and add ば.

Example from this song: あれば (areba) = 'if there is' — from ある (aru, 'to exist') → あれば (areba, 'if there is'). Also: 迷えば (mayoeba) = 'if you get lost' — from 迷う (mayou, 'to lose one's way') → 迷えば (mayoeba)

More examples:
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行けば (ikeba, 'if you go')
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べれば (tabereba, 'if you eat')
• 安い (yasui, 'cheap') → 安ければ (yasukereba, 'if it's cheap')

Note: The ば-conditional often implies a natural or expected consequence: 'if A, then naturally B'. For godan verbs: う→えば, く→けば, す→せば, つ→てば, む→めば, ぶ→べば, ぬ→ねば, る→れば.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: ある (aru, 'to exist') → あれば (areba, 'if there is') / 迷う (mayou, 'to get lost') → 迷えば (mayoeba, 'if you get lost')

grammar_points.name: 〜ながら (while doing)

explanation.en:
How it works: Attach ながら (nagara) to the verb stem (masu-stem) to express doing two actions simultaneously — 'while doing X, also Y'. The main action comes at the end of the sentence.

Example from this song: 傷つきながら (kizutsuki nagara) = 'while getting hurt' — from 傷つく (kizutsuku, 'to get hurt') → 傷つき (kizutsuki, stem) + ながら (nagara, 'while')

More examples:
• 歩く (aruku, 'to walk') → 歩きながら (aruki nagara, 'while walking')
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べながら (tabe nagara, 'while eating')
• 聞く (kiku, 'to listen') → 聞きながら (kiki nagara, 'while listening')

Note: The subject must be the same for both actions. You can't say 'while I walk, he eats'. The verb stem is formed by dropping ます from the polite form: 食べます → 食べ.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 傷つく (kizutsuku, 'to get hurt') → 傷つき (kizutsuki, stem) + ながら (nagara, 'while') → 傷つきながら (kizutsuki nagara, 'while getting hurt')

grammar_points.name: 〜ず(に) (without doing)

explanation.en:
How it works: Change the verb to its negative stem (the ない-form minus ない) and add ず (zu). This means 'without doing X'. Adding に (ni) after is optional and more common in modern Japanese.

Example from this song: 忘れられず (wasurerezu) = 'unable to forget / without being able to forget' — from 忘れる (wasureru, 'to forget') → 忘れられる (wasurerareru, potential: 'can forget') → 忘れられず (wasurerezu, 'without being able to forget')

More examples:
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べず (tabezu, 'without eating')
• 言う (iu, 'to say') → 言わず (iwazu, 'without saying')
• する (suru, 'to do') → せず (sezu, 'without doing') — irregular!

Note: ず is a classical Japanese negative that survives in modern usage. It sounds more literary/poetic than ないで. する → せず is the only irregular form.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 忘れる (wasureru, 'to forget') → 忘れられる (wasurerareru, 'can forget') → 忘れられず (wasurerezu, 'without being able to forget')

grammar_points.name: 意志形 〜よう (volitional)

explanation.en:
How it works: Change the verb ending to express intention or 'let's do'. For -ru verbs (ichidan), replace る with よう. For -u verbs (godan), change the final syllable to its お-row equivalent and add う.

Example from this song: 行こう (ikou) = 'let's go' — from 行く (iku, 'to go') → change く (ku) to こ (ko) + う (u) = 行こう (ikou)

More examples:
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べよう (tabeyou, 'let's eat')
• 見る (miru, 'to see') → 見よう (miyou, 'let's see')
• する (suru, 'to do') → しよう (shiyou, 'let's do it')

Note: For godan verbs: く→こう, す→そう, つ→とう, む→もう, ぶ→ぼう, ぬ→のう, う→おう, る→ろう. The volitional expresses the speaker's will ('I'll do it') or an invitation ('let's do it').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行こう (ikou, 'let's go')

grammar_points.name: 〜にでもなれる (can even become)

explanation.en:
How it works: Combine に (ni, 'into') + でも (demo, 'even') + なれる (nareru, 'can become') to express willingness to become something, even something extreme. It shows determination or desperation.

Example from this song: The song expresses the intensity of being willing to become anything — 'I can even become [something extreme]' — showing the singer's resolve.

More examples:
• 鬼 (oni, 'demon') → 鬼にでもなれる (oni ni demo nareru, 'can even become a demon')
• 何 (nani, 'anything') → 何にでもなれる (nani ni demo nareru, 'can become anything')
• 盾 (tate, 'shield') → 盾にでもなれる (tate ni demo nareru, 'can even become a shield')

Note: でも adds the nuance of 'even' — it emphasizes that the subject is willing to go to that extreme. Without でも, it's simply 'can become'. なれる is the potential form of なる (naru, 'to become').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: なる (naru, 'to become') → なれる (nareru, 'can become') → 鬼にでもなれる (oni ni demo nareru, 'can even become a demon')

grammar_points.name: 〜てやる (do forcefully/for someone)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add てやる (te yaru) after the te-form of a verb to express doing something with determination, defiance, or for someone else (in a rough/masculine way). It shows a strong, aggressive resolve.

Example from this song: The song uses てやる to convey fierce determination — 'I'll definitely do it!' with a defiant edge.

More examples:
• 見る (miru, 'to see') → 見てやる (mite yaru, 'I'll show you / I'll see it through')
• 倒す (taosu, 'to defeat') → 倒してやる (taoshite yaru, 'I'll take you down!')
• 勝つ (katsu, 'to win') → 勝ってやる (katte yaru, 'I'll win, just watch!')

Note: てやる is masculine and assertive. It can mean 'do something for someone' (condescending) or 'I'll definitely do it' (determined). The polite equivalent for doing favors is てあげる (te ageru).

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 倒す (taosu, 'to defeat') → 倒して (taoshite, te-form) + やる (yaru, 'do forcefully') → 倒してやる (taoshite yaru, 'I'll take you down!')
